prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization
Description: The Federal Reserve's monthly G.17 release measures the real output (Industrial Production) and utilization of infrastructure (Capacity Utilization) for U.S. manufacturing, mining, and utilities. It has been designated by the federal government as a Principal Federal Economic Indicator. Utilization rates from the Quarterly Survey of Plant Capacity Utilization (QPC) are a principal source for the measures of capacity and capacity utilization.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization
Description: The Federal Reserve's monthly G.17 release measures the real output (Industrial Production) and utilization of infrastructure (Capacity Utilization) for U.S. manufacturing, mining, and utilities. It has been designated by the federal government as a Principal Federal Economic Indicator. Utilization rates from the Quarterly Survey of Plant Capacity Utilization (QPC) are a principal source for the measures of capacity and capacity utilization.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset comprehensively. Let me start with several searches to verify the details you've provided and gather additional information.# Research Report: Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization (Federal Reserve G.17)

**Report compiled:** October 2026, based on live web research of federalreserve.gov, census.gov, reginfo.gov, the Federal Register, FRED/ALFRED, and OMB documents.

---

## 1. Verification of Your Stated Facts

Your description is accurate, with one useful nuance:

| Your claim | Finding |
|---|---|
| Title: "Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization" | ✅ Confirmed. Officially the "G.17" statistical release (internal series code 419). |
| Published by the Federal Reserve | ✅ Confirmed. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Division of Research and Statistics, Industrial Output (IO) section. |
| Monthly release | ✅ Confirmed. Issued around the 15th of each month at 9:15 a.m. ET, covering the prior month. |
| Measures real output (IP) and capacity utilization for manufacturing, mining, and utilities | ✅ Confirmed — specifically *electric and gas* utilities. |
| Designated a Principal Federal Economic Indicator | ✅ Confirmed. It is one of roughly 35–36 PFEIs designated by OMB under Statistical Policy Directive No. 3. |
| QPC utilization rates are a principal source for capacity measures | ✅ Confirmed with nuance: the Census Bureau's Quarterly Survey of Plant Capacity Utilization is the *primary benchmark source for manufacturing utilization rates* (and an input to IP estimation itself). Capacity for mining and utilities relies on other sources (e.g., Department of Energy data). Per the OMB paperwork clearance, the FRB "uses the data as the primary source of benchmark information for utilization rates as well as an indicator of capital use in the estimation of monthly industrial production." |

---

## 2. Dataset Identity Card

- **Official name:** Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization — G.17
- **Publisher:** Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Washington, DC)
- **Producing unit:** Industrial Output (IO) section, Division of Research and Statistics. Per the Fed's own description, IO "publishes the Federal Reserve's monthly statistical release on Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization (the G.17), a Principal Federal Economic Indicator that makes use of both government and private-sector data sources," conducts industrial-sector analysis and forecasting (motor vehicles, aircraft, oil and gas), and runs the "Expanded Measurement Agenda" using nontraditional data sources.
- **Frequency:** Monthly, ~15 days after the reference month (e.g., May data in mid-June), plus an annual revision (issued at noon, on a pre-announced date).
- **Coverage:** U.S. manufacturing, mining, and electric/gas utilities — the "industrial sector," which the Fed notes, together with construction, "accounts for the bulk of the variation in national output over the course of the business cycle."
- **Time span:** Total industrial production index back to **January 1919** (monthly); capacity and utilization measures back to 1948 (manufacturing) and 1967 (total industry); manufacturing detail on a NAICS basis back to 1972.
- **Base year:** Currently 2017 = 100; the November 2026 annual revision moves the base year to **2022 = 100**.
- **Flagship series on FRED:** INDPRO (Industrial Production: Total Index), TCU (Capacity Utilization: Total Industry), CUMFNS (manufacturing utilization), plus hundreds of industry/market-group series.

---

## 3. Authority, Mandate, and Governance

This is a nuanced area that preservationists and policy activists should understand well, because the G.17's protections are largely **administrative rather than statutory**.

### 3.1 Federal Reserve authority
Unlike the Census Bureau or BLS, the Federal Reserve has no single statute commanding it to publish an industrial production index. The Board produces the G.17 under its general authority in the **Federal Reserve Act of 1913** to conduct research and collect information in support of its monetary policy and economic analysis duties (the Board's broad powers are codified in Section 11 of the Act, 12 U.S.C. § 248, and related provisions). The index was developed in-house beginning in 1922 as an analytical tool — it is a **mission-driven statistical product**, not a congressionally mandated one.

### 3.2 Principal Federal Economic Indicator status
The strongest formal governance comes from **OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3: Compilation, Release, and Evaluation of Principal Federal Economic Indicators** (50 FR 38932, Sept. 25, 1985; updated Feb. 15, 2024, 89 FR 11873). Key obligations:

- **Designation:** The OIRA Administrator designates PFEIs and reviews designations annually. The G.17 is one of ~35–36 series so designated.
- **Prompt release:** Indicators issued quarterly or more frequently must be released within 22 working days of the reference period.
- **Pre-announced schedule:** Release dates are published in advance (the Fed publishes historical release dates back to 1947 and schedules years ahead).
- **Equitable, policy-neutral release:** Strict limits on pre-release access; Executive Branch employees may not publicly comment until **30 minutes** after release (changed from 60 minutes in the 2024 update).
- **Periodic performance evaluation:** Agencies must periodically evaluate each indicator. The Fed files a "Performance Evaluation of the Federal Reserve G.17 (419) Statistical Release" with OMB (the June 2026 evaluation is public on the G.17 site).

**Important caveat for activists:** SPD No. 3 is an OMB directive issued under the Budget and Accounting Procedures Act of 1950 and the Paperwork Reduction Act — it is policy, not statute. The Board is also not one of the "recognized statistical units" under the Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA) in the way Census, BLS, and BEA are. The G.17's integrity rests on the Fed's institutional independence and OMB administrative rules rather than on a dedicated statistical law.

### 3.3 The QPC's legal authority (upstream source data)
The Quarterly Survey of Plant Capacity Utilization is conducted by the **U.S. Census Bureau on behalf of, and co-funded by, the Federal Reserve Board and the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA)**:

- **Authority:** Title 13 U.S.C. § 8(b) (Census's authority to conduct surveys for other agencies, on a cost-reimbursable basis); Title 50 U.S.C. § 98 et seq. (strategic/critical materials authorities relevant to DLA); and Title 12 U.S.C. § 244 (the Federal Reserve Board provision cited as sponsoring authority).
- **Confidentiality:** Title 13 U.S.C. § 9 — responses usable only for statistics, exempt from disclosure, immune from legal process in respondents' files.
- **OMB clearance:** OMB Control No. 0607-0175, Form MQ-C2; ~7,500 respondents; ~30 minutes per response; most recently re-approved July 31, 2024. Response is **voluntary**.
- **Why DLA co-funds it:** DLA uses QPC data "to assess industrial base readiness and ramp-up time to meet demand for goods under selected national emergency scenarios" — the survey collects not just full-capacity but **national-emergency production capability**. Census describes QPC as "the only source for quarterly statistics on U.S. industrial plant capacity."

---

## 4. History

The G.17 is one of the oldest continuously produced U.S. economic statistics — the Fed celebrated the **centennial of the underlying data (1919–2019)** with a dedicated "100 Years" feature on the G.17 site.

### 4.1 Industrial production index lineage
- **1915–1919:** From its founding, the Fed reported business conditions; the first *Federal Reserve Bulletin* (May 1915) carried district business digests, and by 1919 monthly "physical volume of trade" data (tons, feet, etc.) were published — the rootstock of the index.
- **December 1922:** "The Index of Production in Selected Basic Industries" — the first Fed aggregate production index, seasonally adjusted by ratio-to-moving-average, building on Wesley Mitchell's War Industries Board work.
- **1927:** "A New Index of Industrial Production" introduced value-added weights for manufacturing and value-produced weights for minerals, moving seasonal factors, and daily-average output; it "gained wide national acceptance."
- **World War II era:** The index became central to war production planning.
- **1953 revision:** Expanded from 100 to 175 series; monthly indexes benchmarked to comprehensive annual output indexes; value-added weights extended to mining.
- **1959:** Coverage expanded to electric and gas utilities (aligning with UN recommendations); market groups (consumer goods, equipment, materials) introduced; computation computerized.

### 4.2 Capacity utilization lineage
- **Post-WWII–1960s:** The Board began studying capacity and utilization alongside production to analyze demand for capital goods and inflationary pressure. Lacking monthly capacity surveys, staff derived utilization as IP divided by a capacity index.
- **January 1977:** New monthly release **G.3 "Capacity Utilization"** began, with monthly utilization and quarterly output/capacity/utilization for manufacturing and materials.
- **1979:** BLS net capital stock estimates incorporated for materials capacity.
- **1983:** Scope extended to mining and utilities; total-industry estimates backfilled to 1967.
- **April 1990:** G.3 merged with the G.12.3 "Industrial Production" release to form the combined **G.17**, published on or around the 15th.

### 4.3 Modern methodology milestones
- **2002 annual revision:** Cornerstone reclassification from SIC to **NAICS**, with history reconstructed back to 1972 — the first major U.S. economic indicators issued with substantial NAICS history.
- **April 2008:** Six-month estimation window adopted (one new month plus five months of revisions, up from four).
- **2024–2025 annual revisions:** New annual benchmark data for logging, mining, and publishing; 2025 revision incorporated the **2022 Census of Manufactures** and converted the indexes to **2022 NAICS**.
- **2026:** November annual revision rebases to 2022 = 100 and incorporates 2023–2024 Census manufacturing benchmarks.

### 4.4 QPC history (upstream survey)
The plant capacity survey dates to the early 1970s as a Census survey (annual, form MQ-C1), became quarterly (MQ-C2) in the late 1980s, was suspended for part of 2007–2008 amid funding constraints, and resumed in late 2008 under the current FRB/DLA co-sponsorship arrangement. Publishing (NAICS 511) was later added alongside manufacturing. (These dates are from Census/Fed historical documentation; the current quarterly series begins in 2008.)

---

## 5. Content, Scope, and Methodology

### 5.1 What's in the release (typically 18–20 pages plus a detailed supplement)
- **Industrial production indexes** (real output, index form) by:
  - **Market groups:** final products (consumer goods, business equipment, defense/space), nonindustrial supplies, materials — plus stage-of-processing groupings
  - **Industry groups:** manufacturing (durable/nondurable, 3-digit NAICS detail), mining, utilities; special aggregates for high technology, energy, and motor vehicles and parts
- **Capacity indexes** (sustainable potential output) and **capacity utilization rates** (= seasonally adjusted output ÷ capacity) by industry
- **Gross value of industrial products** in billions of chained dollars
- **Diffusion indexes** (breadth of output increases across industries)
- **Supplementary motor vehicle assemblies**
- **Reliability measures** (revision statistics) for total IP and major aggregates

### 5.2 Methodology essentials
- **Index construction:** Fisher (chain-weighted) indexes since 1972, aggregated with value-added weights; detailed series aggregated into market and industry groups.
- **Monthly source data, two types:**
  1. **Physical product data** (tons of steel, barrels of oil, vehicle assemblies) from private trade associations and government agencies — preferred where available;
  2. **Input-based estimates**, primarily **production-worker hours from the BLS establishment survey**, converted to output using productivity factors; (historically, the Fed's own electric-power-use data were used through 1997).
  A few high-tech indexes (e.g., semiconductors) are built by deflating nominal output with Fisher price indexes.
- **Data maturity:** For the first (preliminary, "p") estimate, about **78% of source data** (value-added terms) are in hand; this rises to ~98% by the sixth monthly estimate. Revisions ("r") can continue through annual and benchmark revisions.
- **Benchmarks:** Quinquennial Census of Manufactures and Census of Mineral Industries, Annual Survey of Manufactures (Census Bureau), Minerals Yearbook (USGS), Department of Energy publications, and the QPC for utilization benchmarks.
- **Seasonal adjustment:** Ratio-to-moving-average historically; modern releases use contemporary seasonal adjustment procedures with special treatment for outliers, strikes, hurricanes, and pandemic effects (the releases routinely annotate such special factors — e.g., auto strikes, hurricanes, COVID-19 — making them a rich qualitative record as well).

---

## 6. The Upstream Data Ecosystem (Dependencies)

A preservationist must treat the G.17 not as one dataset but as the apex of a **supply chain**, each link of which is a preservation risk:

1. **Census Bureau:** QPC (voluntary, jointly funded by FRB and DLA — itself a vulnerability, as the 2007 suspension showed); Annual Survey of Manufactures; quinquennial Economic Census.
2. **BLS:** production-worker hours (establishment survey); capital stock estimates. The G.17's methodology has repeatedly changed "in response to either the availability of new data or the discontinuance of previous data sources" (June 2026 OMB evaluation).
3. **Department of Energy / EIA:** electric utility output and generating capacity.
4. **USGS:** minerals data.
5. **Private trade associations:** physical product data (steel, paper, chemicals, autos, etc.). Private data can be discontinued without notice — a recurrent cause of methodology changes and a category that no government archive controls.
6. **Defense Logistics Agency:** co-funder and user of QPC.

---

## 7. Access Points, Formats, and Redistribution

| Channel | Content | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **G.17 web pages** (federalreserve.gov/releases/g17/) | Current release in HTML, PDF, ASCII; monthly supplement; annual revisions; historical release dates back to 1947 | Release archive on site back to **December 1997** |
| **FRASER** (St. Louis Fed) | PDF releases back to **April 1990**; plus Federal Reserve Bulletins with IP data back to 1915 | The key historical archive |
| **Data Download Program (DDP)** | Full time-series downloads (CSV) for all published series, including pre-2000 detail and "100 years" files | ⚠️ **Being discontinued during 2026** — Fed states complete data files will remain on the G.17 site and FRED afterward (see §10) |
| **FRED** (fred.stlouisfed.org) | All major G.17 series (INDPRO, TCU, etc.), with API, Excel/CSV, graphs | The dominant public access route |
| **ALFRED** (alfred.stlouisfed.org) | **Vintage ("real-time") data**: every historical revision of the series as it existed on each release date, back to **1927** — reconstructed from historical publications | Invaluable for research on revisions, nowcasting, and policy history |
| **Third parties** | Bloomberg, Haver, OECD, IMF, trading platforms | Broad secondary mirroring aids resilience |

**Licensing:** The data are U.S. government-produced statistics, freely redistributable; the Fed and FRED request only attribution. No registration or fees.

---

## 8. Users and Use Cases

Documented in the Fed's OMB performance evaluations and elsewhere:

- **Monetary policy:** The FOMC and Fed staff use IP/capacity as core gauges of real activity, resource slack, and inflation pressure — historically, sustained high utilization has been read as an inflationary warning sign.
- **Financial markets:** A scheduled, market-moving PFEI; the 2024 SPD No. 3 update explicitly analyzed how futures markets price PFEI releases within minutes.
- **Other statistical agencies:**
  - **BEA** uses IP indexes in the national income and product accounts (investment in computers and peripheral equipment, transportation equipment inventories, proprietors' income, rental income).
  - **BLS** uses production indexes to estimate manufacturing productivity.
- **Forecasting:** The Atlanta Fed's **GDPNow** nowcast consumes IP indexes; IP is a standard input to private nowcasting/forecasting models.
- **Business cycle dating:** IP is one of the key monthly indicators considered by the **NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee** in identifying recession peaks and troughs.
- **Defense planning:** Via QPC, DLA assesses industrial-base surge readiness.
- **Business and labor:** Industry-level IP/utilization inform capacity investment, pricing, and negotiations.
- **Academia and education:** One of the most-cited U.S. macro time series; the long 1919–present span supports business-cycle and structural-change research.
- **Media and the public:** Widely reported monthly as a headline read on the factory economy.

## 9. Public Benefits

1. **Timeliness with integrity:** First estimate ~15 days after month-end under a legally constrained, pre-announced, politically insulated release process.
2. **A 107-year consistent series:** The reconstructed NAICS history (back to 1972) and 1919 total index are irreplaceable for studying long-run structural change, depressions, wars, and deindustrialization.
3. **Free, open, machine-readable access** via FRED/API — a model of open government data that underpins countless downstream products.
4. **Accountability infrastructure:** PFEI status forces regular public performance evaluations and advance announcement of methodology changes — transparency mechanisms preservationists can leverage.
5. **National security value:** QPC-linked capacity data support emergency preparedness, a benefit rarely visible to the public.
6. **Cross-agency multiplier:** The same dataset feeds GDP estimation, productivity statistics, and nowcasts — discontinuation would degrade multiple other federal statistics.

---

## 10. Preservation Assessment and Risks

**Current developments of direct concern to preservationists:**

- ⚠️ **DDP retirement (in progress, 2026).** The Fed's Data Download Program is being discontinued over the course of 2026; "Build Your Own Data Package" functionality was already being removed (week of November 9 announcement). The Fed commits to posting complete release files on the G.17 site and continuing FRED distribution, but **bulk download structures, pre-2000 discontinued series, and the DDP's particular metadata layouts should be captured now** before removal.
- **Structural risks:**
  - No statutory mandate — production could theoretically be curtailed by internal Fed budget/priority decisions (compare the QPC's actual 2007 suspension for funding reasons).
  - PFEI protections are OMB policy, revisable by notice.
  - Heavy dependence on upstream series (BLS hours, Census surveys, trade association data) — degradation anywhere in the chain degrades the G.17.
  - The QPC is voluntary and depends on continued FRB/DLA co-funding.
- **Mitigants (unusually strong redundancy):** FRASER's release archive to 1990 and Bulletin scans to 1915; ALFRED's vintage archive to 1927; FRED mirroring; extensive commercial/academic redistribution; End of Term Web Archive crawls of federalreserve.gov; the Board's own published revision files.
- **Recommended actions for a preservationist:**
  1. Snapshot the DDP bulk files and pre-2000 series before decommissioning is complete.
  2. Archive the G.17 HTML/PDF/ASCII release pages and methodology/history pages (the HistIP/HistCap histories and "100 Years" feature are not fully mirrored elsewhere).
  3. Preserve OMB performance evaluations and annual revision documentation — they are the authoritative record of methodology changes.
  4. Rely on ALFRED for vintage data rather than attempting to reconstruct revisions from raw releases.
  5. Monitor the QPC's OMB clearance cycle (No. 0607-0175) at reginfo.gov as an early-warning indicator of upstream risk.

---

## 11. Key Sources

- G.17 home, about page, and methodology: federalreserve.gov/releases/g17/ (About, HistIP, HistCap, ipnotes, release_dates)
- Performance Evaluation of the G.17 (June 2026): federalreserve.gov/releases/g17/OMB/2026/
- Industrial Output section description: federalreserve.gov/econres/rsio-staff.htm
- OMB SPD No. 3: 50 FR 38932 (1985); update at 89 FR 11873 (Feb. 15, 2024); BLS copy at bls.gov/bls/statistical-policy-directive-3.pdf
- QPC: census.gov/programs-surveys/qpc.html; OMB ICR at reginfo.gov (Control No. 0607-0175, ICR 202403-0607-006); Federal Register notice 89 FR (Mar. 27, 2024)
- FRED/ALFRED: fred.stlouisfed.org/series/INDPRO; alfred.stlouisfed.org/release?rid=13
- FRASER: fraser.stlouisfed.org (release archive from April 1990; Federal Reserve Bulletin from 1915)

---

**Assessment date:** October 2026, based on live research of federalreserve.gov, reginfo.gov, FRED/ALFRED, the Federal Register, and news coverage.

**Overall context:** This dataset sits in an unusual position. The G.17 itself has continued operating without interruption to its content, but three shocks in the past 18 months shape the risk picture: (1) the fall 2025 government shutdown delayed two releases by weeks; (2) the Fed announced a ~10% system-wide staff reduction in May 2025; and (3) an unprecedented political pressure campaign against the Federal Reserve and federal economic statistics (firing of the BLS Commissioner, attempted removal of a Fed Governor, DOJ investigation of the Chair, and a contested leadership transition to Kevin Warsh in May 2026). None of these has yet altered the G.17's content — but several rubric categories are behavior- and environment-based, and they score accordingly.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone / High Risk:* No evidence. No historical G.17 releases, series, or vintages have been removed from any known location.
- *Moderate Risk:* One borderline item — the Fed is retiring the **Data Download Program (DDP)** during 2026 and removed the "Build Your Own Data Package" functionality. This is an access *tool*, not a data element, and the Fed has publicly committed that complete data files will remain posted on the G.17 site and on FRED. However, DDP-specific artifacts (pre-2000 discontinued series layouts, bulk package structures) could be lost in the transition if the commitment is not fully executed.
- *No Known Issue:* Monthly release archive intact on federalreserve.gov back to **December 1997** (HTML/PDF/ASCII); FRASER holds releases back to **April 1990** and Federal Reserve Bulletins with IP data back to **1915**; **ALFRED** preserves every vintage of the series back to **1927**; FRED carries the full series to 1919. Extensive third-party mirroring (Bloomberg, Haver, OECD) adds redundancy. Release dates page documents an unbroken publication history back to 1947.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** All prior-cycle data remain publicly accessible with no known alterations. Preservationists should nonetheless snapshot DDP bulk files now, before the 2026 decommissioning completes, as a precaution.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone:* No — collection and publication continue; the most recent monthly release was September 18, 2026, with the next scheduled October 16, 2026, and a full pre-announced schedule through December 2027.
- *High Risk:* No statutory publication deadline exists to miss (the G.17 is not statutorily mandated), and the key upstream ICR is current: QPC (OMB Control No. **0607-0175**, Form MQ-C2) was re-approved July 31, 2024, **expiration 07/31/2027**, status Active (reginfo.gov, ICR 202403-0607-006).
- *Moderate Risk:* **Publication delays did occur.** Due to the fall 2025 federal government shutdown delaying source data from BLS and Census, the G.17 releases scheduled for **October 17, 2025 and November 18, 2025 were not published as scheduled**; they were ultimately issued December 3 and December 23, 2025 (with the December release combined), per the Fed's own notices (federalreserve.gov/feeds/g17.html and the December 3, 2025 release text). This squarely matches the rubric's "typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed." Publication has since returned to schedule.
- *No Known Issue:* Would apply on the strength of the active ICR and on-schedule 2026 releases — but the rubric is behavioral, and the missed dates are recent, documented fact.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Two intended publication dates were missed within the past year. Mitigating factors: the cause was upstream (shutdown), not internal to the Fed; the Fed communicated transparently and caught up within weeks; no cycle was skipped entirely. The episode does, however, demonstrate the release's structural dependence on other agencies' data flows — a recurrence pathway that remains open.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone / High Risk:* No reduction in the G.17's own granularity, timeliness, or frequency. The release retains full NAICS industry and market-group detail, diffusion indexes, and reliability statistics; monthly frequency and the ~15-day lag are unchanged; the annual revision is proceeding on schedule (November 24, 2026, with rebase to 2022=100 and incorporation of 2023–2024 Census benchmarks — an *improvement* in currency).
- *Moderate Risk:* **Emerging risks to the input supply chain are documented:**
  - **BLS turmoil:** President Trump fired BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer on August 1, 2025, accusing her without evidence of rigging data (AP, Reuters, NYT). Production-worker hours from the BLS establishment survey are the *primary monthly source* for most manufacturing IP series. Politicization or degradation of BLS survey operations (also strained by declining response rates and staffing losses) directly threatens G.17 input quality.
  - **Shutdown demonstrated fragility:** the October–November 2025 delays show the release cannot be produced when upstream agencies stop publishing.
  - **QPC dependence:** the manufacturing utilization benchmark survey is voluntary, jointly funded by the FRB and DLA — an arrangement that failed once before (survey suspended 2007–08) and depends on continued co-funding.
  - **Fed staff reductions** (below) create capacity risk for the small Industrial Output section.
- *No Known Issue:* Applies only to the G.17 product as published to date — but "potential or emerging risk" is clearly present in the ecosystem.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The dataset's own specifications are maintained or improving, but credible, documented threats to the granularity and timeliness of its essential inputs (BLS hours, Census surveys) have emerged since January 2025.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence by level:**
- *High Risk (partial match):* Statutory authorization is indeed **vague** — no statute names the G.17; it is produced under the Board's general Federal Reserve Act powers (12 U.S.C. § 248). However, the other High Risk prongs fail: there are **no true alternative data collections** that could substitute (private proxies like the ISM PMI are diffusion surveys, not real-output indexes), and programmatic use is extensive and documented (FOMC monetary policy deliberations; BEA uses IP in GDP/NIPA estimates; BLS uses IP for productivity statistics; NBER business-cycle dating; DLA industrial-base planning via the QPC).
- *Moderate Risk (best fit):* "Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a federal program, and no substitutes." The G.17 is not statutorily mandated by name, but it is operationally embedded in the Fed's statutory monetary policy mission, in BEA's statutory national accounts, and in BLS productivity measurement. Its **Principal Federal Economic Indicator** designation under OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3 provides administrative (not statutory) protection: pre-announced schedules, release-integrity rules, and mandatory periodic performance evaluations. The upstream QPC has *explicit* statutory authority (13 U.S.C. § 8(b); 12 U.S.C. § 244; 50 U.S.C. § 98 et seq.) and Title 13 confidentiality — but it is the input, not the G.17 itself.
- *No Known Issue:* Does not apply — no statute explicitly requires this collection.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The dataset's protection is administrative and institutional rather than statutory, which is precisely why it is exposed to internal Fed budget decisions and political pressure — but its deep, irreplaceable integration into GDP estimation, productivity statistics, and monetary policy makes outright termination highly improbable.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone:* No. The Industrial Output section exists and is producing; QPC funding continues.
- *High Risk (40%+ staff loss, 1,000+ lost, 20%+ budget cut, leadership removed):* Not met for the Fed as publisher. The announced reduction is ~10% of ~24,000 system-wide (~2,400 positions) **over several years, mainly through attrition** and a voluntary deferred resignation program limited to Board staff eligible to retire by end-2027 (Powell memo, May 16, 2025; Reuters/Bloomberg/NYT). That is ~2,400 positions planned, which *numerically* exceeds the "1,000 or more staff lost" threshold — but the rubric thresholds read most naturally on losses already realized, and these are phased, voluntary, and attrition-based, with an explicit commitment in the memo to "prioritize and safeguard our ability to meet our Congressionally mandated mission." The Fed is **self-funded** (no appropriated budget to cut). On leadership: Chair Powell was *replaced at the end of his term* by Kevin Warsh (confirmed 54–45, May 13, 2026) — a transition under extreme pressure but through the normal process. The attempt to *remove* Governor Lisa Cook was **blocked by the Supreme Court (June 2026)**; a renewed removal effort began in August 2026 and is unresolved, and reporting (CNBC, Oct. 1, 2026) indicates as many as three governors could be targeted.
- *Moderate Risk (best fit):* "10–39% of staff lost" — a planned **10%** system-wide reduction sits at the bottom of this band; and "threatened change in leadership" is amply documented: threats to fire Powell (Guardian, April 2026), the DOJ investigation of Powell (quashed by Judge Boasberg as pretextual), and the ongoing Cook removal effort. No evidence the IO section or statistical production has been specifically targeted, and the QPC's FRB/DLA co-funding has not been cut.
- *No Known Issue:* Not applicable given the announced 10% reduction and leadership turmoil.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** A 10% workforce reduction is planned (at the low end of the band and attrition-based), and leadership threats are real though so far legally constrained. Escalation to High Risk would be warranted if the Cook removal succeeds, if the efficiency review reaches statistical production units, or if the BLS (upstream) experiences further decapitation — note BLS Commissioner McEntarfer's firing already satisfies "leadership removed" for a key *input* agency, which is captured under Data Quality.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone:* No.
- *High Risk:* Not met. The QPC ICR is a routine renewal, not a Presidential Action-driven collection; there is no negative policy note on the G.17 site; no Administration-priority-driven change to the release's content has occurred.
- *Moderate Risk:* Partially arguable — Administration officials have made statements attacking federal economic statistics generally (Trump's "rigged data" claims justifying the BLS firing; Hassett defending the dismissal) and attacking the Fed as an institution. However, **no official has proposed or suggested changing what the G.17 specifically collects or publishes**, and no such change is pending. The dataset-specific trigger in the rubric ("statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned" *to this data*) is not met.
- *No Known Issue (best fit):* Since January 2025, there have been **no notable changes affecting what data the G.17 collects and publishes** — same tables, same industry detail, same methodology, same schedule (shutdown delay aside, which was an operational pause, not a policy change). The 2026 annual revision is a routine, pre-announced methodological improvement, not a policy change.

**Assessment: No Known Issue** — for the dataset itself. This is the narrowest reading of the rubric, and it should be paired with an explicit caveat: the Administration's demonstrated willingness to fire a statistical agency head over unfavorable numbers, and its pressure campaign against the Fed, mean the *environmental* policy risk to federal economic statistics is elevated. Because the G.17 lacks statutory protection (see Statutory Context), a policy-driven change could be executed quickly if the institution's insulation erodes. Preservationists should treat Policy as "No Known Issue, actively monitored."

## Summary of Risk Levels

- **Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue** — archives intact across Fed site, FRASER, FRED, and ALFRED; snapshot DDP bulk files before its 2026 retirement completes.
- **Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk** — two scheduled releases missed in late 2025 due to the government shutdown (caught up by Dec. 23, 2025); QPC ICR active through July 31, 2027; releases on schedule through 2026 with dates announced through 2027.
- **Data Quality: Moderate Risk** — the G.17's own granularity/timeliness/frequency are maintained (2026 rebase proceeding), but emerging, documented threats to essential upstream inputs: BLS leadership firing and institutional stress, Census funding pressure, and the shutdown-proven fragility of the multi-agency data chain.
- **Statutory Context: Moderate Risk** — not statutorily mandated (general Federal Reserve Act authority + OMB SPD No. 3 administrative designation), but deeply embedded in federal programs (GDP, productivity, monetary policy) with no substitute collections.
- **Staffing and Funding: Moderate Risk** — planned ~10% system-wide staff reduction (attrition-based, phased through 2027); intense but so far legally checked leadership threats (Powell→Warsh transition May 2026; Cook removal blocked by Supreme Court, renewed August 2026); Fed self-funding limits budget-cut exposure.
- **Policy: No Known Issue** — no changes to what the G.17 collects or publishes since January 2025; elevated general politicization of economic statistics warrants active monitoring given the dataset's lack of statutory shielding.

**Overall:** The G.17 is among the more resilient federal datasets — self-funded publisher, century-long continuity, massive third-party redundancy, and deep programmatic embeddedness — but its 2025–2026 experience shows that its greatest vulnerability is not internal: it is the **upstream statistical system** (BLS, Census) and the **political environment** surrounding the Federal Reserve. The most actionable preservation step remains securing the DDP-era bulk files and monitoring the QPC clearance cycle and Fed staffing decisions as early-warning indicators.
